newsitem.title: USA: Army rape defendant's lawyers focus on women's pasts.
newsitem.headline: Army rape defendant's lawyers focus on women's pasts.

text.p: Lawyers for Army rape defendant Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, in a closed court hearing Thursday, sought approval to introduce at his upcoming trial evidence related to past behaviour of his alleged victims.

The request indicated his lawyers might argue that any relationships Simpson had were consensual, echoing media reports that the Aberdeen Proving Ground where he was based had a climate of pervasive sexual activity.

"I think that by the time all the witnesses have testified, both government and defence, I think that everyone will have a fairly accurate picture of what's been going on at Aberdeen Proving Ground," Simpson's civilian attorney Frank Spinner told reporters after the hearing.
Simpson faces a total of 138 counts of sexual misconduct and other crimes, including charges that he raped 10 female trainees.

Simpson would be the first of 10 soldiers charged in a major sexual misconduct scandal at the Aberdeen Proving Ground to go to trial. The trial is scheduled to start April 14, preceded by jury selection next week.

An article in the Washington Post Sunday, based on interviews and court records, described the Aberdeen base as having a climate of unusually pervasive sexual activity among trainees and between traineers and their superiors.

Asked if he would argue that Simpson only engaged in consensual sex, Spinner said, "we'll discuss what pleas will be entered at another time." "Our position is that Sgt. Simpson did not rape anyone," he said earlier.

But Spinner said it would be hard to paint in court a "broad brush" argument based on the base's sexual climate, because military court rules require that any evidence of a witness's sexual behaviour must be relevant to the specific issues of the case.
There was no decision yet on that issue.

Simpson is charged with violating the federal Sexual Abuse Act of 1986 through 16 counts of sexual intercourse by fear involving seven women, and three counts of sodomy by fear involving two women. He is also charged under military rape and sodomy laws for the same incidents and others.
Military code allows prosecutors to charge soldiers governed by military law with federal crimes unless Congress indicates military law takes precedence.
Prosecutor Capt. Theresa Gallagher said if Simpson were convicted under both laws, prosecutors would ask to dismiss the federal charges.
Spinner argued that legal precedent in military law allowed for a broader definition of force that would make it indistinguishable from the federal law.

He said after the hearing the military was trying to try Simpson doubly for the same incident, in part for publicity purposes. "I think it's clear that they're trying to make the case look worse than it was," he said.
